summary: This paper investigates how language models retrieve bound entities in-context, challenging the prevailing positional-only view by identifying two additional mechanisms—lexical and reflexive—that compensate when the positional mechanism degrades for middle-position entities. The authors build a clean causal model combining all three mechanisms that achieves 95% JSS agreement with LM behavior and validate their account across 9 models and 10 tasks. The core contributions are genuine and the methodology is rigorous, but the causal model is only comprehensively evaluated on one or two models in the main text, several unexplained 'mixed' cases remain unaccounted for, and the generalization to naturalistic text is more a characterization of degradation than a robustness positive.
strengths: The three-mechanism taxonomy (positional, lexical, reflexive) is well-motivated, clean, and covers a gap that prior work explicitly acknowledged—prior work on binding either restricted to n≤3 or achieved low causal faithfulness at larger n.

The counterfactual dataset design (Section 3.2) is elegant: the originals and counterfactuals are constructed so that all three mechanisms predict distinct outputs, enabling clean causal attribution, and the reflexive-mechanism validation in 3.4 (modified counterfactual where the answer entity is absent from context) is a particularly rigorous sanity check.

Scale of evaluation is appropriate for ICLR: nine models across three families (Gemma-2, Qwen-2.5, Llama-3.1) spanning 2B–72B, plus ten templatic binding tasks, and a free-form filler-token generalization experiment.

The causal model (Section 4) achieves JSS 0.95 vs. 0.44 for the positional-only prevailing view—below even a uniform baseline—and the learned Gaussian width σ(iP) as a quadratic function of relative position is a satisfying, interpretable formalization of the diffuseness observation.

The connection to the 'lost-in-the-middle' effect (Liu et al., 2024) as a mechanistic consequence of a weakening lexical mechanism relative to a noisy positional one is a concrete, testable hypothesis that extends the paper's contribution beyond its immediate scope.

key_concerns.issue: The causal model (Section 4, Figure 5) is evaluated comprehensively only on gemma-2-2b-it (music task), with qwen2.5-7b-it on additional tasks deferred to Appendix E. Given that nine models are used for the mechanism analysis, restricting full causal model evaluation to one or two models makes it difficult to assess whether the Gaussian positional term and learned lexical/reflexive weights generalize across architectures and families.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report causal model JSS and KL results for all nine models (or at minimum one model per family at each scale tier) in the main text as a compact table, even if some ablations remain in the appendix.

key_concerns.issue: The 'mixed' category in Figures 2–3 accounts for a substantial fraction of predictions in middle positions, but receives only qualitative characterization (distributed near the positional index). There is no mechanistic account of what produces these predictions or why they fall outside all three hypothesized mechanisms, leaving a gap in the proposed complete picture.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either extend the causal model to cover the mixed cases (e.g., as superpositions or a fourth regime), or provide a more systematic characterization—e.g., are mixed cases predominantly due to attention head noise, position aliasing, or model-specific failure modes—so that the '95% agreement' claim is not qualified by an unexplained residual.

key_concerns.issue: Multiple citations throughout the methods sections are anonymized as '[Author] et al.' including for the causal abstraction framework and interchange intervention methodology that the paper is fundamentally built on. While double-blind preparation explains the redaction, it makes it impossible to evaluate whether the contribution is sufficiently differentiated from the authors' prior work, and whether methodological choices are independently validated or self-referential.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: In the camera-ready version, restore these citations and add an explicit paragraph delineating what this paper adds beyond the prior causal abstraction work. As a reviewer note: this is flagged as a deanonymization artifact, not as grounds for rejection.

key_concerns.issue: The generalization experiment (Section 5, Figure 6) is framed as demonstrating robustness in 'more natural settings,' but the binding structure itself remains fully synthetic—only filler sentences are added between entity groups. The lexical mechanism actually declines monotonically with padding, and positional information nearly disappears for the first half of entity tokens at 10,000 filler tokens. This is better characterized as a stress test revealing mechanism degradation than as generalization evidence.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Reframe Section 5 as a parametric stress test with a finding that mechanisms degrade in a predictable order, connecting it to the lost-in-the-middle hypothesis. The current framing as robustness overclaims relative to the evidence.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical reporting for the causal model is incomplete in the main text. The caption for Figure 5 states CIs < 0.02 (and < 0.002 for M and oracle), but does not report confidence intervals for all ablations, the method for computing CIs, or the number of random seeds. It is unclear whether JSS differences between ablations (e.g., 0.94 vs. 0.91) are statistically significant.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report 95% CIs uniformly across all rows of Figure 5, specify the CI computation method (bootstrap, analytic), and add a brief note on whether key differences between ablations are statistically distinguishable.

key_concerns.issue: The reflexive mechanism is motivated as necessary when the target entity precedes the query entity in a group (tentity < qentity), because attention cannot look forward. However, the main experiments use tentity ∈ {1, 2, 3} in groups of size m=3, meaning the forward-attention constraint applies to tentity ∈ {1, 2} but not tentity = 3. The reflexive mechanism's contribution for tentity = 3 cases (visible in Figure 5 ablation row) is not explained.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a brief discussion of why the reflexive mechanism contributes even for tentity = m, possibly involving indirect retrieval paths or attention over previously retrieved tokens.

questions_for_authors: Figure 2 shows a U-shaped distribution of mechanism contributions across entity group indices. Does this U-shape emerge regardless of n, or does it require a minimum n to appear? Figure A.3 apparently shows this, but the main text would benefit from a brief characterization of the threshold.

The causal model weights wlex and wref are conditioned on iL and iR respectively (learned per-index weights). How many parameters does the full model M have, and is there a risk of overfitting given n^3 = 8,000 training+validation+test distributions constructed from 150 interventions per combination?

For the padding experiment in Section 5, was the causal model re-fit to padded inputs, or is Figure 6 showing how the original model trained on clean inputs transfers to padded ones? The answer substantially affects the interpretation.

The 'competitive synergy' described in Section 3.3—lexical and positional mechanisms boosting/suppressing each other depending on proximity, while lexical is suppressed by reflexive when close—is intriguing. Is this interaction captured by the additive causal model in Equation 2, or is the equation a simplification that omits interaction terms?

The limitations section mentions that 'some comparisons are made against a limited set of alternatives, and a broader baseline set could change the relative ordering.' Can you be more specific about which comparisons are most at risk and what alternative hypotheses you considered but did not fully test?
calibration_check: The central quantitative claim—95% JSS agreement between the causal model and LM behavior—is well-supported by Figure 5 for gemma-2-2b-it, but its generality across all nine models is asserted rather than shown in the main text; the framing of the filler-token experiment as generalization to naturalistic settings is somewhat overstated given the continued synthetic binding structure.

significance.justification: The paper makes a meaningful contribution to mechanistic interpretability by extending the binding/retrieval account from trivially small settings to realistic multi-entity contexts and connecting the mechanism degradation to the well-known lost-in-the-middle effect; researchers in interpretability and long-context reasoning will find it directly relevant.

novelty.justification: The lexical and reflexive mechanisms are genuinely new proposals with empirical support, and the three-mechanism causal mixture model is a novel formalization; the methodology (interchange interventions, causal abstraction) is established prior work, but its application to distinguish and quantify mechanism contributions at scale is a non-trivial extension.

rigor.justification: The counterfactual design in Sections 3.2 and 3.4 is careful and the reflexive-mechanism validation is well-executed, but the causal model evaluation is concentrated on one model in the main text, the 'mixed' prediction category lacks a mechanistic account, and the interaction effects in Section 3.3 are described qualitatively without formal characterization.

statistical_soundness.justification: CIs are stated to be below 0.02 for the main causal model results, and 150 interventions per combination for n^3=8,000 distributions is a reasonable sample size, but CI reporting is inconsistent across ablations, the method for computing CIs is not stated, and significance of differences between ablation rows is not assessed.

calibration_honesty.justification: The paper honestly characterizes the positional mechanism's limitations and acknowledges the mixed-prediction residual; the limitations section is genuine though somewhat vague; the framing of the filler-token experiment as generalization slightly overclaims relative to the evidence of mechanism degradation.

clarity.justification: The paper is well-written, the three-mechanism taxonomy is clearly defined, and the counterfactual logic is explained step by step; some notation overloading (tentity, qgroup, iP/iL/iR) accumulates across sections and requires close reading, and the [Author] redactions interrupt the flow of the related work discussion.

structure_compliance.justification: The paper follows standard conference structure with a clear method section, experiments section, and limitations; the appendix is used appropriately for additional model/task replication; length appears within ICLR norms based on the 10 main-text pages visible.

reproducibility.justification: Model identifiers, task templates (via appendix), and data collection procedure (150 interventions per combination, 70/15/15 split) are stated; however, optimization details for the causal model (optimizer, learning rate, number of runs), the specific layer-selection procedure for the nine models, and the entity vocabulary sizes are not fully specified in the main text.

related_work.justification: The paper engages substantively with the entity-binding literature (Prakash et al., Dai et al., Feng & Steinhardt, Wu et al.) and correctly characterizes the gap (prior work limited to n≤3 or low faithfulness at n=7); the [Author] et al. redactions make it impossible to evaluate positioning relative to the authors' own prior causal abstraction and interchange intervention work, which is a meaningful gap.

figure_quality.justification: Based on captions, the figures are designed to directly support the claims: Figure 2's U-shaped mechanism distribution, Figure 3's Gaussian diffuseness of the positional mechanism, Figure 5's JSS comparison table, and Figure 4's reflexive mechanism validation all correspond to specific quantitative claims; the combination of confusion matrices, logit distributions, and weight visualizations provides appropriately varied evidence.

breadth_generality.justification: Nine models across three families and ten binding tasks is a solid experimental footprint for mechanistic interpretability, but the causal model fitting and ablations are shown for one primary model in the main text, the free-form text experiment uses only one model on one task, and the scope is limited to decoder-only transformer architectures with standard instruction-tuning.

overall_recommendation.justification: This is a solid mechanistic interpretability paper that genuinely advances understanding of in-context entity binding beyond prior narrow settings; the three-mechanism account is well-validated and the causal model is a useful contribution, but the restricted causal model evaluation, unexplained mixed predictions, and overstated generalization slightly weaken the overall case for acceptance without revision.
